summary: The note describes how intramural swimming leagues in Tokyo's community pools have grown into an organized local sports scene with neighborhood teams, Saturday meets, and strong social bonds. It profiles swimmers, team captains, a referee, a council member and a physician, and covers the leagues' benefits for community pride, local businesses, schools and health. Upcoming rivalry between teams such as the Aoyama Angels and Setagaya Swimmers is highlighted.
one_line: Tokyo's community pool intramural swimming leagues foster rivalry, fitness, community bonds and local pride through neighborhood teams and weekend meets.
key_facts: Shinjuku Central Swimming Complex hosted the inaugural swim meet of the season on September 15, 2023.
City officials recognize the health and social benefits of the intramural leagues and have provided resources and support to expand them.
Sachiko Tanaka is a 42-year-old marketing consultant and mother of two who competes in 100m freestyle heats; she says "It's not just about swimming."
The Shinagawa Sharks are led by former Olympic swimmer Takeshi Kobayashi and are known for emphasis on technique and speed.
The Meguro Mermaids, captained by Yuki Nakamura, focus more on endurance and strategy and create an inclusive environment for various skill levels.
A Tuesday training session was observed on September 25, 2023.
Hiromi Sato, a 28-year-old graphic designer on the Shibuya Stingrays, says her team became a second family and gave her friends, support and self-confidence.
Saturday meets feature colorful banners and concession stands selling takoyaki (octopus balls) and yakisoba (fried noodles).
Age categories let participants from schoolchildren to seniors compete.
Kenjiro Watanabe, a 56-year-old former schoolteacher, volunteers as a referee at the meets.
An October 10th meet is anticipated between the Aoyama Angels, known for precision and cohesion, and the Setagaya Swimmers, known for relay strength.
Schools have seen increased participation in swim programs, and local businesses benefit from visitors on meet days.
Council member Akira Fujimoto said at Toshima Pool Complex: "Not only are we creating better swimmers; we are strengthening communities."
Ken Matsuda, a 34-year-old architect on the Minato Marlins, used to swim alone with headphones on and now values the team community.
Dr. Miyu Oshima, a local physician, says regular swimming lowers chronic disease risk and improves mental health and resilience.
